title: CUTLASS Array vector slices use a start and count, not a Python stop index
applies_when: A CuTeDSL cutlass.Array explicit vector slice looks empty or too short at a nonzero offset, or a proposed FlashInfer accumulator repair substitutes Python list slicing semantics.
lesson: Trace the receiver's construction and pinned __getitem__/__setitem__ contract first. This CUTLASS Array implements arr[start:count] for explicit vector loads and stores: acc[offset:4] transfers four elements at a nonzero offset. Changing it to acc[offset:offset+4] changes the count rather than repairing a Python stop index. FlashInfer's cited acc_list contains these Array objects; a Python-list surrogate cannot test their semantics. Inspect the real operation and caller before proposing a slice rewrite.
avoid_when: Only the cited explicit start/count vector form and revisions are established here. Open-ended or multidimensional slices, other receiver classes and dependency versions require separate inspection. Syntax alone does not prove bounds, alignment, synchronization, generated-kernel correctness or performance. A genuine native failure can still justify a repair; this counterexample rejects only the built-in-list premise.

evidence.note: The vector-load branch uses the slice's second value as an element count and its first as the pointer offset; the Vector-store branch at L2664-L2685 follows the same convention. This is a pinned vendor source contract, not an installed dependency or GPU-kernel test.
acc_list constructs cutlass.Array objects; _acc_g[_o:4] is written at L932 and read at L970. This connects the receiver to the vendor contract, not whole-kernel correctness or performance.
